topic: Vulnerability discovery in Electron-framework desktop applications (and closely adjacent mechanisms)

include: Electron apps (VS Code, Slack, Teams, Discord, etc.) security/vulnerabilities
nodeIntegration, contextIsolation, sandbox, preload/contextBridge, remote module
Chromium Embedded Framework (CEF), WebView-based desktop apps, hybrid web/desktop apps
DOM-based / XSS->RCE escalation into local privileges in desktop apps
npm / supply-chain issues as they affect Electron or the Node.js runtime
exclude: pure web-app XSS with no desktop/Electron angle
generic Chromium browser bugs unrelated to embedded/desktop apps

_keyword_blind_spot_2026_09_06: A USENIX Security '23 paper squarely inside the INCLUDE rule — 'Bilingual Problems: Studying the Security Risks Incurred by Native Extensions in Scripting Languages' (Staicu et al., CISPA) — survived SIX runs of this watch undetected, because its title contains NONE of the keywords above: not 'electron', not 'node.js', not 'npm', not 'supply chain'. It was caught only as a side effect of a domain-restricted WebSearch ('Electron desktop application vulnerability detection', allowed_domains usenix.org + the other venue hosts), which surfaces papers by TOPICAL relevance rather than by title keyword. TWO CONSEQUENCES, both now standing practice: (1) the keywords.native_boundary_added_2026_09_06 list above covers the JS<->C/C++ boundary, which the original keyword set omitted entirely; (2) THE DOMAIN-RESTRICTED TOPICAL SWEEP IS NOW A REQUIRED CHANNEL, not an optional one — run it every time, because it is the only channel in this watch that can find a correctly-scoped paper whose title shares no vocabulary with the config. Assume other backfill misses of the same shape remain in 2020-2025; rotate the domain-restricted sweep across different scope phrasings on successive runs.

discovery_method._tooling_constraints_2026_09_04: TWO HARD LIMITS discovered this run, both of which cost budget if rediscovered. (1) web_fetch enforces a PROVENANCE SET: it will only retrieve a URL that literally appeared in a user message, a previous web_fetch result, or a WebSearch result. You CANNOT construct a URL — not from this config, not by adding ?page=N. Templated URLs in the 'venues' list above must therefore be surfaced by a WebSearch first (search the page title, e.g. "USENIX Security '26 technical sessions"), THEN fetched. (2) The built-in browser pane requires per-site approval, which a scheduled non-interactive run cannot grant: navigation to raid2026.org and dblp.org both returned 'denied or failed'. So the DBLP-TOC channel and any JS-rendered accepted-papers page are UNAVAILABLE in scheduled runs — they need an interactive session. CONSEQUENCE for large venues: the USENIX '26 technical-sessions page is paginated and one fetch yields only ~54 of ~400 titles with no way to page forward. Substitute a domain-restricted WebSearch (allowed_domains usenix.org) using the scope keywords; that is the workable exhaustive-ish channel for big programs.

domain_restricted_topical_sweep.why: The only channel that finds correctly-scoped papers whose titles share no vocabulary with the keyword list — see _keyword_blind_spot_2026_09_06. Produced the Bilingual Problems (USENIX Sec '23) catch on its first use, and NatiSand (RAID '23) + the 'Extending a Hand to Attackers' exclusion on its second (2026-09-07). THIRD USE, 2026-09-08: produced 'Too Much of a Good Thing: (In-)Security of Mandatory Security Software for Financial Services in South Korea' (USENIX Sec '25) — a top-4 paper, in the backfill window, invisible to every keyword channel because its title contains none of the config vocabulary. That is now THREE consecutive runs in which this channel, and only this channel, produced a correctly-scoped backfill miss. TWO LESSONS ON QUERY WORDING: (a) 'inter-process communication privilege boundary application' returned almost nothing but US patents — abstract OS-systems phrasing pulls the patent corpus, not security venues, so keep the wording APPLICATION-SHAPED ('desktop application', 'web content', 'renderer', 'add-on') rather than OS-primitive-shaped ('IPC', 'privilege boundary'). (b) The two productive queries this run both named a CONCRETE ARCHITECTURE ('untrusted web content renderer', 'local HTTP server desktop agent'). Prefer architecture nouns over mechanism nouns. The rotation list has been extended to ten queries and 'not_yet_used' emptied; treat the list as a ring buffer and consult 'queries_used_so_far' to pick the least-recently-used two or three each run. FOURTH USE, 2026-09-09: ALL THREE remaining unused queries were fired and the channel produced NOTHING new — the first null result in four runs. The results were dominated by pre-2020 classics (Protecting Browsers from Extension Vulnerabilities NDSS'10, JSand ACSAC'12, The Effectiveness of Application Permissions WebApps'11) and, for two of the three queries, by US PATENTS and PL-theory papers. This CONFIRMS AND SHARPENS the 2026-09-08 wording lesson: 'attack surface measurement' and 'foreign function interface' are METRIC/MECHANISM nouns and they pull the patent + programming-languages corpus, exactly as 'inter-process communication privilege boundary' did. The rotation list is now fully consumed once. WHEN REFILLING IT, write ARCHITECTURE-SHAPED queries in the style of the two that actually worked ('sandbox escape desktop application untrusted web content renderer', 'local HTTP server desktop agent web page privileged API security study') — name a concrete component ('preload script', 'auto-updater', 'custom protocol handler', 'deep link', 'notification bridge', 'packaged app bundle') rather than an abstract property. Suggested next-round queries: 'custom URL scheme handler desktop application attack', 'auto-update mechanism desktop client integrity study', 'deep link handling native application web origin', 'markdown renderer desktop note-taking application injection', 'chat client link preview server-side request'. One null run is NOT yet evidence of backfill convergence — it is one data point, and it was spent on the three weakest-worded queries in the buffer. FIFTH USE, 2026-09-10: NULL for a second consecutive run, and it re-confirms the wording rule a third time. The five queries fired were the config's own suggested refills plus two of my own. 'custom URL scheme handler desktop application attack' returned almost entirely US PATENTS - 'URL scheme handler' reads as a MECHANISM noun to the search index despite sounding architectural. 'markdown renderer desktop note-taking application injection' returned scattered unrelated USENIX/ACM papers with no topical cluster at all. 'auto-update mechanism desktop client integrity study' returned exactly one target-venue paper and it was ALREADY EXCLUDED (When Updates Backfire, USENIX Sec'26). 'deep link handling ...' returned only mobile/Android deep-link work (all pre-2020 or already excluded). 'preload script contextBridge renderer main process desktop app study' returned Inspectron - already in_scope - which is a POSITIVE control: the channel does surface the right cluster when one exists, so the nulls are informative rather than tooling failures. SHARPENED RULE: a query is architecture-shaped only if the named component is one a DEVELOPER WOULD NAME IN AN APP'S SOURCE (preload script, auto-updater, link preview, drag-and-drop handler), not one an OS or spec would name (URL scheme, IPC, FFI, deep link). TWO NULL RUNS IN A ROW IS NOW THE FIRST WEAK EVIDENCE OF CONVERGENCE FOR THIS CHANNEL - but note that on both runs the OTHER required channel (related-work / author-page mining) produced in_scope papers, so the backfill itself has NOT converged.

related_work_mining.why: PROVEN ON ITS FIRST USE. The domain-restricted sweep found NatiSand (RAID '23); reading NatiSand's §8 Related Work then yielded BinWrap (AsiaCCS '23, DISTINGUISHED PAPER, squarely in scope, never seen by six prior runs) as reference [14], plus Cage4Deno and an eBPF/Wasm poster (both AsiaCCS '23) as [2] and [1]. Backfill misses cluster: a paper the watch missed is written by and cites people the watch also missed, so one catch is a thread that pulls several more. Author-page mining is the same idea and is cheap — the Bergamo (unibg seclab) and Brown (Kemerlis/Vasilakis) groups are now known-productive in this exact niche. PROVEN AGAIN 2026-09-08, on the paper found by the previous run's mining. BinWrap's bibliography yielded TWO first-time in_scope triages — Mir (CCS '21, reference [72]) and Cross-Language Attacks (NDSS '22, reference [41]) — plus two exclusions recorded so they are never re-chased (sysfilter, RAID '20, ref [18]; NodeSentry, ACSAC '14, ref [17], topically in scope but out on the backfill_from_year=2020 rule). The chain is now four links long: domain-restricted sweep -> NatiSand (RAID '23) -> BinWrap (AsiaCCS '23) -> Mir (CCS '21) + Cross-Language Attacks (NDSS '22). MINE EVERY NEWLY ADDED PAPER'S BIBLIOGRAPHY, INCLUDING PAPERS THAT WERE THEMSELVES FOUND BY MINING. FOURTH CONSECUTIVE PRODUCTIVE RUN, 2026-09-09, but with a TWIST that changes the method: the yield came from AUTHOR-PAGE mining, not reference-list mining. Mir's reference [76] pointed at Harp, but the fastest and most complete route was to open the first author's publications page, which listed Harp, Pitchfork (ACSAC'22, excluded), SecBench.js (ICSE'23, context) and Lexo (arXiv, context) in one fetch. Meanwhile the OTHER pending bibliography (Cross-Language Attacks NDSS'22) yielded ZERO in_scope papers. CONCLUSION: prefer author-page mining over bibliography mining when the newly added paper has a distinctive author group, and mine PRIMARY-tagged papers' bibliographies before ADJACENT-tagged ones.
related_work_mining.how: For EVERY paper newly added to in_scope, fetch its related-work / references section and check each cited work against (a) the nine venues and (b) the scope rules. Record the disposition of every cited venue paper checked, including exclusions, so the same references are not re-chased next run.

AUTHOR-PAGE MINING, PROVEN 2026-09-09: nikos.vasilak.is/publications (also atlas.cs.brown.edu/publications) is a single page listing the ENTIRE Vasilakis output with direct author-hosted PDFs, and it produced Harp (CCS'21) faster and more reliably than chasing Mir's reference [76] would have. It also surfaced two context items now in the ledger (SecBench.js ICSE'23; Lexo arXiv 2025) and one exclusion (Pitchfork ACSAC'22). PDF URL pattern is nikos.vasilak.is/p/<slug>:<venue>:<year>.pdf — but remember the web_fetch provenance rule: fetch the publications page FIRST, then follow the links inside it. Kemerlis (Brown) next; they are the two remaining hubs of this collaboration network whose author pages this watch has never opened.

CISPA - Cristian-Alexandru Staicu's group, MINED 2026-09-10 at staicu.org/publications: the single highest-yield author page of this watch. Beyond Bilingual Problems it produced SandDriller (USENIX Sec'23) and Welcome to Jurassic Park (NDSS'25), both in_scope, plus CHARON (EuroS&P'25, context). His PhD student ABDULLAH ALHAMDAN is first author on both new finds and works exactly on JS-runtime isolation/permission auditing - track him by name in future sweeps. Note also the Staicu<->Vasilakis<->Pradel overlap (Mir CCS'21, SecBench.js ICSE'23) confirming these are one extended network.
